objectives.1.4: Data management and privacy in AI

questions.question: A security team trains a model on 50,000 emails, each tagged by analysts as 'phishing' or 'legitimate', so it can classify new emails. Which machine learning paradigm is this?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Self-supervised learning
questions.answer: Supervised learning
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labeled input-output pairs, here emails plus analyst-assigned labels. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, reinforcement learning learns from rewards in an environment, and self-supervised learning creates its own labels from the data (as in LLM next-token prediction). Because the labels drive what the model learns, label integrity is a security concern: label flipping is a common poisoning technique against supervised models.

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)
references.section: 2.1.1 Stages of Learning (learning methods: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, etc.)

questions.question: An autonomous agent learns a network-defense policy by receiving positive feedback when it blocks attacks and negative feedback when it disrupts legitimate traffic. Which paradigm does this describe?
options: Supervised learning
Transfer learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
questions.answer: Reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent through trial and error, using reward signals from its environment rather than labeled examples. A key security risk is reward hacking: the agent finds a way to maximize reward that doesn't match the designer's intent, such as blocking all traffic so it never misses an attack. Transfer learning reuses a model trained on one task as the starting point for another.

references.title: Amodei et al., Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016)
NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: Unsupervised learning techniques such as clustering can flag anomalous network behavior without needing labeled examples of past attacks.
options: True
False
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods find patterns and outliers in unlabeled data, which makes them useful for anomaly detection when novel attacks have no labels yet. The tradeoff is a higher false-positive rate, because 'unusual' is not always 'malicious', so results usually need analyst review.

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: Which neural network architecture relies on a self-attention mechanism and underpins most modern large language models?
options: Convolutional neural network (CNN)
Recurrent neural network (RNN)
Generative adversarial network (GAN)
Transformer
questions.answer: Transformer
questions.explanation: Transformers, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', use self-attention to weigh the relationships between all tokens in a sequence in parallel. They replaced RNNs for most language tasks because RNNs process tokens one at a time and struggle with long-range dependencies. CNNs excel at spatial data such as images; GANs pair two networks to generate synthetic data.

references.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
references.section: Section 3.2: Attention (3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention, 3.2.2 Multi-Head Attention)

questions.question: In a generative adversarial network (GAN), the discriminator creates synthetic samples while the generator tries to tell real samples from fake ones.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: The roles are reversed. The generator creates synthetic samples and the discriminator tries to distinguish them from real data; each improves by competing with the other. GANs matter for security because they can produce deepfakes, and they can also generate adversarial examples or synthetic training data.

references.title: Goodfellow et al., Generative Adversarial Nets (2014)

questions.question: Why are GPUs generally preferred over CPUs for training deep neural networks?
options: GPUs have higher clock speeds than CPUs
GPUs include built-in hardware encryption for model weights
GPUs have thousands of cores optimized for parallel matrix and vector operations
GPUs can train models without using system memory
questions.answer: GPUs have thousands of cores optimized for parallel matrix and vector operations
questions.explanation: Training is dominated by large matrix multiplications that can be split across many simple cores running in parallel. CPUs have fewer, more powerful cores built for sequential, general-purpose work, and they usually run at higher clock speeds than GPUs. Specialized accelerators such as TPUs and NPUs push the same idea further.

references.title: NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide

questions.question: An organization runs AI workloads for several business units on shared GPU accelerators. Which security risk is specific to this setup?
options: Residual data left in GPU memory may be readable by a later workload from another tenant
GPU firmware cannot be patched, so vulnerabilities are permanent
Shared GPUs prevent the use of TLS for API traffic
GPU workloads cannot be logged by a SIEM
questions.answer: Residual data left in GPU memory may be readable by a later workload from another tenant
questions.explanation: GPU memory is not always cleared between jobs. The LeftoverLocals vulnerability (CVE-2023-4969, disclosed in 2024) showed that on some Apple, AMD and Qualcomm GPUs one process could read another's local GPU memory, including fragments of LLM responses. Mitigations include dedicated or isolated accelerators for sensitive work, memory scrubbing between jobs, and patched drivers and firmware. The other options are false: GPU drivers and firmware can be patched, and TLS and logging are unaffected.

references.title: Trail of Bits, LeftoverLocals: Listening to LLM responses through leaked GPU local memory (CVE-2023-4969), Jan 2024
references.section: Full post, including the mitigation guidance

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
options: To permanently update a model's weights with new documents
To ground the model's responses in relevant external information retrieved at query time, without retraining
To compress a model so it runs on edge devices
To encrypt prompts before they are sent to the model
questions.answer: To ground the model's responses in relevant external information retrieved at query time, without retraining
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant content, often from a vector database, and adds it to the prompt so the model can answer from current or proprietary information. The model's weights don't change; fine-tuning is what changes weights, and compression covers techniques like quantization and pruning. RAG brings its own risks: retrieved content is a prompt injection channel, and the retriever must respect the user's access permissions.

references.title: Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (NeurIPS 2020)
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
references.section: Description; Prevention and Mitigation Strategies 1: Permission and access control

questions.question: An attacker plants a document containing hidden instructions on an internal wiki that a RAG-based assistant indexes. When an employee's question retrieves that document, the assistant follows the hidden instructions and leaks data. What is this attack?
options: Direct prompt injection
Model inversion
Indirect prompt injection
Membership inference
questions.answer: Indirect prompt injection
questions.explanation: In indirect prompt injection, the malicious instructions arrive through content the model processes (web pages, emails, documents, tool results) rather than being typed by the user. Direct prompt injection is when the user supplies the malicious prompt themselves. Because LLMs cannot reliably separate instructions from data, defenses include treating retrieved content as untrusted, limiting what the assistant can do with it, and filtering outputs.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection

references.title: MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0051.001 LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect

questions.question: Which fine-tuning method freezes the original model weights and trains small low-rank matrices inserted into selected layers?
options: Full fine-tuning
Knowledge distillation
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)
questions.answer: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)
questions.explanation: LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method: it trains a small number of added parameters, which makes fine-tuning far cheaper than updating every weight. Full fine-tuning updates all weights, RLHF aligns a model using human preference rankings, and distillation trains a smaller 'student' model to imitate a larger 'teacher'. LoRA adapters are small, easily shared files, so they need the same provenance checks as full models: a malicious adapter can introduce a backdoor.

references.title: Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (2021)
references.section: Section 4: Our Method (4.1 Low-Rank-Parametrized Update Matrices)

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning
references.section: Description (poisoning of fine-tuning data to introduce backdoors)

questions.question: In the context of language models, what is an embedding?
options: A cryptographic hash of a document used to detect tampering
A dense numeric vector that represents the meaning of content, so similar content sits close together
A watermark inserted into generated text
A compressed copy of the model's weights
questions.answer: A dense numeric vector that represents the meaning of content, so similar content sits close together
questions.explanation: Embeddings map text, images or audio into a high-dimensional vector space where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness. Vector databases store embeddings and use similarity search to power RAG. Unlike a hash, an embedding is designed to preserve meaning, which is why it can leak information about its source.

references.title: Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Embeddings: Embedding space and static embeddings
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses

questions.question: Embeddings stored in a vector database are a one-way transformation, so they cannot reveal information about the original source text.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Embedding inversion research (for example Vec2Text, 2023) showed that much of the original text can be reconstructed from its embedding. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 lists Vector and Embedding Weaknesses as LLM08. Protect a vector database as you would the source data: encryption, access controls, and partitioning by tenant or permission level.

references.title: Morris et al., Text Embeddings Reveal (Almost) As Much As Text (EMNLP 2023)
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
references.section: Common Examples of Risks 3: Embedding Inversion Attacks

questions.question: A model is advertised with a 128,000-token context window. What does this limit?
options: The number of words the model was trained on
The number of users who can query the model at once
The number of parameters in the model
The total number of tokens the model can consider at once, including instructions, user input, retrieved content and conversation history
questions.answer: The total number of tokens the model can consider at once, including instructions, user input, retrieved content and conversation history
questions.explanation: Tokens are the units a model processes, often word fragments; one token is roughly three-quarters of an English word. The context window caps how many tokens fit in one request. Security relevance: very large inputs drive cost and can cause denial of service (OWASP LLM10 Unbounded Consumption), and instructions buried in long context are harder to spot.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption
references.section: Common Examples of Vulnerability 1 and 3: Variable-Length Input Flood, Continuous Input Overflow

questions.question: What most distinguishes an agentic AI system from a standard chat assistant?
options: It can plan multi-step tasks and take actions through tools and APIs with limited human involvement
It always uses a larger model
It only answers questions from a fixed FAQ
It cannot access the internet
questions.answer: It can plan multi-step tasks and take actions through tools and APIs with limited human involvement
questions.explanation: Agents combine a model with planning, memory and tool use, so they can act: send email, run code, change records. That autonomy widens the attack surface, because a prompt injection against an agent can trigger real actions. This is why OWASP lists Excessive Agency (LLM06) and why agents need least-privilege tool permissions and human approval for high-impact steps.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
references.section: Description; Common Examples of Risks: excessive functionality, permissions, autonomy

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: A system prompt is a reliable security boundary: instructions placed in it cannot be revealed or overridden by user input.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: System prompts can be extracted or overridden through prompt injection and jailbreaks; OWASP lists System Prompt Leakage as LLM07:2025. Never put secrets such as API keys in a system prompt, and enforce access control and authorization in deterministic code outside the model.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
references.section: Description; Prevention and Mitigation Strategies 1 and 4

questions.question: An attacker hides low-contrast text instructions in an image that a person is unlikely to notice. A vision-language assistant reads the text and follows it. What does this demonstrate?
options: Image inputs are automatically sanitized by model providers
Only text inputs can carry prompt injection
Any input modality a multimodal model accepts can carry a prompt injection
The attack requires access to the model's weights
questions.answer: Any input modality a multimodal model accepts can carry a prompt injection
questions.explanation: Multimodal models turn images, audio and documents into the same internal representation as text, so instructions can hide in any of them. Input filters that only inspect text miss these attacks. Defenses include treating all external content as untrusted, scanning images (for example with OCR), and limiting the actions the model can take based on that content.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
references.section: Description (multimodal risks); Example Attack Scenario #7: Multimodal Injection

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: A legal research assistant built on an LLM cites a court case that does not exist. Which limitation does this show?
options: Concept drift
Hallucination (confabulation)
Overfitting
Model collapse
questions.answer: Hallucination (confabulation)
questions.explanation: LLMs generate plausible text; unless grounded, they don't look facts up, so they can produce fluent, confident fabrications. Lawyers have been sanctioned for filing briefs with AI-invented citations. Mitigations include RAG grounding, automated citation checks, and human review for high-stakes output. OWASP covers this as Misinformation (LLM09).

references.title: NIST AI 600-1, AI RMF: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (July 2024)
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM09:2025 Misinformation
references.section: Common Examples of Risk 2: Unsupported Claims; Prevention and Mitigation Strategies

questions.question: A fraud detection model's input features look statistically the same as at training time, but its accuracy drops because fraudsters changed tactics, so the same patterns now mean something different. What is this?
options: Data (covariate) drift
Model collapse
Label leakage
Concept drift
questions.answer: Concept drift
questions.explanation: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between the inputs and the correct output. Data drift (covariate shift) is a change in the input distribution itself. Both erode performance over time, so production models need ongoing monitoring against fresh labeled data, with thresholds that trigger retraining or reassessment. In security, drift is often adversarial: attackers adapt to evade the model.

references.title: Gama et al., A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation, ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), 2014
references.section: Section 1: Introduction (real concept drift vs. changes in the input distribution)

questions.question: Model collapse is a degradation that can occur when generative models are repeatedly trained on content produced by other AI models, causing them to lose rare patterns from the original data.
options: True
False
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: Research published in Nature in 2024 (Shumailov et al.) showed that recursively training on model-generated data makes models forget the 'tails' of the real distribution, so outputs become less diverse and less accurate over generations. As more web content is AI-generated, tracking data provenance and keeping human-generated data in training sets matters more.

references.title: Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data, Nature 631 (2024)

questions.question: An intrusion detection model is tested on traffic where 1% of connections are malicious, and it scores 99% accuracy. Why might this result be misleading?
options: Accuracy cannot be calculated for binary classifiers
A model that labels every connection benign would also score 99%, so precision and recall are more informative
99% accuracy always means the model is overfitted
Accuracy measures only false positives
questions.answer: A model that labels every connection benign would also score 99%, so precision and recall are more informative
questions.explanation: With heavily imbalanced classes, accuracy is dominated by the majority class. Precision (of the items flagged, how many are truly malicious), recall (of the truly malicious items, how many were caught), F1 and precision-recall curves give a truer picture. Security data is almost always imbalanced, so always ask which metric a vendor's headline number refers to.

references.title: Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Classification: Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics
references.section: Accuracy (imbalanced datasets); Choice of metric and tradeoffs

questions.question: For a malware detection model, the team's top priority is to miss as few real malware samples as possible, even if analysts see more false positives. Which metric should they optimize?
options: Precision
Specificity
Recall
Accuracy
questions.answer: Recall
questions.explanation: Recall (sensitivity, or true positive rate) = TP / (TP + FN): the share of actual malware that gets caught. Raising recall usually lowers precision, which means more false positives and more analyst workload. Precision = TP / (TP + FP); specificity measures how well benign files are correctly cleared.

references.title: Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Classification: Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics
references.section: Recall, or true positive rate; Precision

questions.question: In which oversight model does a human supervise an AI system that acts on its own and intervene only when needed, rather than approving each decision?
options: Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
Human-on-the-loop (HOTL)
Human-out-of-the-loop
Two-person integrity
questions.answer: Human-on-the-loop (HOTL)
questions.explanation: In HOTL, the system acts autonomously while a human monitors it and can override or halt it. In HITL, a human must review or approve each decision before it takes effect. Human-out-of-the-loop means full autonomy with no real-time oversight. Match the model to impact: high-impact or irreversible actions usually warrant HITL, while HOTL suits high-volume, lower-risk decisions backed by good monitoring.

references.title: European Commission High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (2019)
references.section: Chapter II, Requirement 1: Human agency and oversight (Human oversight: HITL, HOTL, HIC)

questions.question: A high score on a well-known public benchmark guarantees that a model will perform equally well on an organization's specific use case.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Benchmarks measure performance on a fixed test set that may not resemble your data, and popular benchmarks can leak into training data (contamination), inflating scores. Evaluate models on representative, held-out data from your own use case, including adversarial and edge-case tests, before deployment.

references.title: Sainz et al., NLP Evaluation in trouble: On the Need to Measure LLM Data Contamination for each Benchmark (Findings of EMNLP 2023)

questions.question: Which technique adds calibrated statistical noise so that an analysis or trained model reveals almost nothing about whether any single individual's record was included?
options: Tokenization
Differential privacy
k-anonymity
Homomorphic encryption
questions.answer: Differential privacy
questions.explanation: Differential privacy (DP) gives a mathematical guarantee controlled by a privacy budget, epsilon: the smaller epsilon, the stronger the privacy and the larger the accuracy cost. DP-SGD applies it during model training and helps defend against membership inference. k-anonymity generalizes records so each matches at least k-1 others; tokenization swaps sensitive values for surrogates.

references.title: NIST SP 800-226, Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees (March 2025)
references.section: Privacy parameter (epsilon) and the differential privacy pyramid

references.title: NIST SP 800-188, De-Identifying Government Datasets: Techniques and Governance (Sept 2023)

questions.question: Several hospitals want to train a shared diagnostic model without moving patient records outside each hospital. Which approach best fits?
options: Consolidating the records into a shared data lake
Transfer learning
Federated learning
Publishing a shared synthetic dataset
questions.answer: Federated learning
questions.explanation: In federated learning, each participant trains locally and shares only model updates, which a central server aggregates; raw data never leaves its site. Updates can still leak information or be poisoned by a malicious participant, so federated learning is often combined with secure aggregation, differential privacy and robust aggregation methods.

references.title: Kairouz et al., Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning (2021)
references.section: Section 4: Preserving the Privacy of User Data; Section 5: Defending Against Attacks and Failures

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
references.section: Prevention and Mitigation Strategies: Federated Learning and Privacy Techniques

questions.question: Which technique allows computation directly on encrypted data, so the system doing the processing never sees the plaintext?
options: Trusted execution environment (TEE)
Differential privacy
Data masking
Homomorphic encryption
questions.answer: Homomorphic encryption
questions.explanation: Homomorphic encryption lets a party compute on ciphertext and return an encrypted result that only the key holder can decrypt; it remains computationally expensive, especially for large models. A TEE is different: data is decrypted, but only inside a hardware-isolated enclave. Differential privacy adds noise, and masking hides values without allowing computation on the originals.

references.title: NIST SP 800-188, De-Identifying Government Datasets: Techniques and Governance (Sept 2023)
references.section: 3.9.2 Secure Computation (fully homomorphic encryption); 3.9.3 Trusted Execution Environments

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
references.section: Prevention and Mitigation Strategies: Advanced Techniques (homomorphic encryption)

questions.question: What does data provenance provide for an AI training dataset?
options: A guarantee that the data is free of bias
Encryption of the data at rest
A record of where the data came from, who owns it, and how it was transformed over its lifecycle
A single score measuring data quality
questions.answer: A record of where the data came from, who owns it, and how it was transformed over its lifecycle
questions.explanation: Provenance documents origin, ownership, licensing and every transformation. That supports trust, reproducibility, legal compliance and incident investigation, for example tracing which source introduced poisoned data. Provenance doesn't prove data is accurate or unbiased, but you can't properly assess either without it.

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning
references.section: Prevention and Mitigation Strategies 1: track data origins and transformations (OWASP CycloneDX, ML-BOM)

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM03:2025 Supply Chain

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of unstructured data?
options: A relational table of payment transactions
A JSON API response with defined fields
A collection of recorded customer support calls
A CSV file of sensor readings with fixed columns
questions.answer: A collection of recorded customer support calls
questions.explanation: Unstructured data, such as audio, images, video and free text, has no predefined schema. Relational tables and fixed-column CSVs are structured; JSON and XML are semi-structured, carrying keys or tags without a rigid schema. Unstructured data is harder to classify and scan for sensitive content, and it makes up much of what generative AI ingests.

references.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: unstructured data

questions.question: Removing direct identifiers such as names and Social Security numbers from a dataset is enough to prevent individuals from being re-identified.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Quasi-identifiers can still single people out: Latanya Sweeney's research found that ZIP code, birth date and sex alone uniquely identify roughly 87% of the US population. Strong de-identification combines removing direct identifiers with generalization, suppression, k-anonymity or differential privacy, plus a re-identification risk assessment.

references.title: Sweeney, L., Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely, Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3 (2000)
references.section: Abstract; Section 2.1: Linking to re-identify de-identified data

references.title: NIST SP 800-188, De-Identifying Government Datasets: Techniques and Governance (Sept 2023)
references.section: 4.3 De-Identification by Removing Identifiers and Transforming Quasi-Identifiers

questions.question: Synthetic data produced by a model trained on real customer records carries no privacy risk, because it contains no real records.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Generative models can memorize and reproduce parts of their training data, especially rare or duplicated records, so synthetic output can leak real personal information. Validate synthetic data before use: test for memorization and near-duplicates, and consider training the generator with differential privacy.

references.title: NIST SP 800-188, De-Identifying Government Datasets: Techniques and Governance (Sept 2023)
references.section: 4.4 Synthetic Data (4.4.7 Creating a Synthetic Dataset with Differential Privacy)

references.title: Carlini et al., Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models, USENIX Security 2021

questions.question: Which framework is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI-enabled systems, modeled on MITRE ATT&CK?
options: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
ISO/IEC 42001
MITRE ATLAS
OWASP SAMM
questions.answer: MITRE ATLAS
questions.explanation: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) catalogs real-world tactics, techniques and case studies of attacks on ML systems in an ATT&CK-style matrix. The NIST AI RMF is a risk management framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), ISO/IEC 42001 is an AI management system standard, and OWASP SAMM is a software assurance maturity model.

references.title: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems)

questions.question: An attacker queries a facial recognition API many times and uses the returned confidence scores to reconstruct a recognizable image of a person in the training set. Which attack is this?
options: Membership inference
Model inversion
Model extraction
Evasion
questions.answer: Model inversion
questions.explanation: Model inversion reconstructs representative features or samples of the training data from a model's outputs. Membership inference only determines whether a specific record was in the training set, model extraction steals the model's functionality, and evasion fools the model at inference time. Defenses include returning labels instead of detailed confidence scores, rate limiting, and training with differential privacy.

references.title: Fredrikson, Jha, Ristenpart, Model Inversion Attacks that Exploit Confidence Information and Basic Countermeasures, ACM CCS 2015
MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0024.001 Invert AI Model
NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: Model extraction (model stealing) attacks require the attacker to first obtain the model's weights file.
options: True
False
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: Extraction usually works through the public query interface: the attacker sends many inputs, records the outputs, and trains a substitute model that mimics the target. The copy can then be used to compete with the owner or to craft adversarial examples offline. Controls include rate limiting, monitoring for unusual query patterns, limiting output detail, and watermarking.

references.title: Tramer et al., Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs, USENIX Security 2016
MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0024.002 Extract AI Model
NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)

questions.question: An attacker makes small, carefully chosen changes to a malware file so an ML-based detector classifies it as benign, while the malware still works. What type of attack is this?
options: Data poisoning
Backdoor insertion
Model inversion
Evasion (adversarial example)
questions.answer: Evasion (adversarial example)
questions.explanation: Evasion attacks happen at inference time: they modify inputs to cross the model's decision boundary without changing the model. Poisoning and backdoors happen at training time by corrupting what the model learns. Defenses include adversarial training, input transformations, ensembles of diverse detectors, and not relying on a single ML control.

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)
MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0015 Evade AI Model

questions.question: An attacker slips training samples containing a small trigger pattern, all labeled with a chosen class, into a dataset. The trained model performs normally on clean inputs but outputs the attacker's class whenever the trigger appears. What is this?
options: Evasion attack
Backdoor (trojan) attack
Availability poisoning
Membership inference
questions.answer: Backdoor (trojan) attack
questions.explanation: A backdoor is a targeted poisoning attack that implants hidden behavior activated by a trigger. Because performance on clean data looks normal, standard accuracy testing won't reveal it. Availability poisoning, by contrast, aims to degrade the model's overall performance. Mitigations include data provenance, dataset inspection and outlier detection, and dedicated backdoor-scanning tools.

references.title: NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025)
Gu, Dolan-Gavitt, Garg, BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain (2017)
MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0020 Training Data Poisoning

questions.question: Applying Zero Trust principles to an LLM-based agent most directly means:
options: Trusting the agent fully once it authenticates at startup
Placing the agent inside the corporate network perimeter
Treating the agent's requests as untrusted and verifying each action with least-privilege, per-request authorization
Relying on the system prompt to restrict what the agent can do
questions.answer: Treating the agent's requests as untrusted and verifying each action with least-privilege, per-request authorization
questions.explanation: Zero Trust means never trust, always verify: every request is authenticated and authorized based on identity and context, and access is kept minimal. For AI, the model and its outputs are untrusted, each tool call is checked against policy, credentials are scoped and short-lived, and the agent gains no implicit trust from its network location or from instructions in its prompt.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of an output guardrail for an LLM application?
options: Rate limiting login attempts to the application
Scanning the model's responses for personal data and secrets and redacting them before they reach the user
Checking user prompts for known jailbreak patterns
Fine-tuning the model on more training data
questions.answer: Scanning the model's responses for personal data and secrets and redacting them before they reach the user
questions.explanation: Output guardrails inspect and filter what the model produces, for example redacting PII, blocking harmful content, or validating structured output before it's passed to another system. Reading the description on the model card
Verifying its cryptographic signature or hash against the value published by the trusted publisher

options: Automatically closing all low-severity alerts without any review
Replacing SIEM correlation rules entirely
Summarizing and enriching alerts so analysts can triage faster, with analysts making the final call
Making firewall changes on its own based on threat intelligence feeds

The assistant cannot read PDF files
Users will need to reset their passwords

It removes the need for attackers to send email at all
It only affects voice phishing

Retraining the model on demand whenever they disagree with it
Approving every single inference in real time before any output is released
